The bug pattern is premature scalarization of AVX-512 mask values from k-registers to GPRs even though the immediate hot-path consumer is a mask-only kortest. Builtin expansion is exactly where intrinsics like _mm256_cmpeq_epu16_mask, _kortestz_mask16_u8, and later scalar mask uses get lowered into RTL, so a flawed expansion can easily force early kmov materialization that later scheduling cannot undo cleanly.

This is the strongest candidate. The bug is a backend quality issue in final hot-path code shape after registers have been assigned: two kmovw instructions remain before kortestw even though only the cold path needs scalar mask values. A post-reload combine/simplification pass is exactly where GCC could recognize that the branch can stay entirely in k-registers and sink or avoid one/both kmov materializations until the match-found path. Because the problem is not semantic correctness but poor final placement/combination in the inner loop, reload_combine is the most likely best fix location among the listed methods.

behavior_items: The function implements a vectorized search over a char16_t range [n, e) looking for the first occurrence of a 16-bit character c. It broadcasts c into a 256-bit AVX register so that each loop iteration can compare many elements against the same target in parallel.

Each loop iteration advances n by 32 char16_t elements. Because char16_t is 2 bytes, that corresponds to 64 bytes per iteration, split into two 32-byte unaligned loads: data1 loads elements n..n+15 and data2 loads elements n+16..n+31.
The loads use _mm256_loadu_si256, so the reproducer exercises GCC's AVX2/AVX-512 code generation for unaligned 256-bit memory accesses. These become vmovdqu16 loads in the shown assembly.

The comparisons use _mm256_cmpeq_epu16_mask on each loaded vector against the broadcast target. Instead of producing a full vector result, these intrinsics produce AVX-512 mask-register results (__mmask16), one bit per 16-bit lane. mask1 describes matches in the first 16 elements and mask2 describes matches in the second 16 elements.

The first control decision is expressed as _kortestz_mask16_u8(mask1, mask2). Semantically, this checks whether the bitwise AND of the two masks is zero according to the kortest condition exposed by the intrinsic; in this search pattern it is being used as a fast mask-only branch to skip the expensive index-finding path when no relevant match condition is detected for the current block.

At the machine-code level, the important point is that this early branch can be decided entirely in mask registers. The masks are already produced in k-registers by the vector compares, and kortestw can test those k-registers directly without first copying them into general-purpose integer registers.

If the early test indicates no candidate match for the current 32-element block, the loop continues immediately with the next block. This makes the no-match path the hot path, so the reproducer is specifically sensitive to any unnecessary instructions inserted before the branch.

If the block may contain a match, the function computes the index of the first set bit in mask1 using _tzcnt_u32. This finds the first matching element among the first 16 lanes. The use of tzcnt makes the reproducer exercise the transition from AVX-512 mask values into scalar integer bit operations.

The subsequent if (mask1 == 0) handles the case where the first match was not in the first half. If mask1 is zero, the code computes the trailing-zero count from mask2 instead and adds 16 elements to n so that returning n + idx still yields the correct pointer into the second half of the 32-element block.

The function returns immediately upon finding the first match in the current block, preserving strstr-like first-occurrence semantics. If the loop finishes with no match before reaching e, it returns e as a sentinel meaning 'not found in range'.

The bug report focuses not on functional miscompilation but on poor instruction selection/scheduling in the hot no-match path. GCC emits two kmovw instructions immediately after producing the two masks: one copies k0 to edx and the other copies k1 to eax.

Those kmovw moves are unnecessary for the subsequent kortestw itself, because kortestw operates directly on k-register operands. In the shown sequence, the branch decision could have been made immediately after the two vpcmpuw instructions, as Clang demonstrates.

The likely reason GCC materializes the masks in general-purpose registers is that later code needs scalar forms of mask1 and mask2 for tzcnt and the mask1 == 0 test. However, doing both kmovw instructions eagerly on the hot path lengthens the dependency chain before the branch and penalizes the common case where the loop simply continues.

The performance issue is microarchitectural: on the target x86 implementation discussed in the report, kmovw and kortestw contend for the same execution resources, specifically port 0. Because GCC places two kmovw instructions before kortestw, the kortest cannot issue until those moves complete, creating an avoidable delay.

According to the report's LLVM-MCA analysis, this scheduling increases the steady-state loop cost from about 2 cycles per iteration to about 3 cycles per iteration. Since the loop is a scan over memory where many iterations often contain no match, a 1-cycle regression in the inner loop is significant.

Clang's generated loop avoids the problem by keeping the hot-path control test entirely in mask registers: compare into k0/k1, then kortestw k0,k1, then branch. This preserves a shorter critical path and better throughput.

ICC reportedly emits only one kmovw before the branch. The report notes that this is still able to sustain about 2 cycles per iteration because that single move can overlap with other work such as one of the loads, unlike GCC's two serially competing kmovw instructions.

The reproducer therefore exercises a specific compiler backend quality issue: GCC recognizes the AVX-512 mask operations correctly and produces functionally valid code, but it schedules or lowers mask-to-GPR transfers too early, before the branch that could have been resolved solely in mask registers.

This is a classic hot-path/cold-path placement problem. The scalarized mask values are only needed on the taken path where a match exists and tzcnt must locate it, but GCC hoists their production into the common no-match path, degrading performance without changing observable program behavior.

In summary, the code is a high-throughput 16-bit character search using two 256-bit compares per iteration, AVX-512 mask registers for match detection, and scalar tzcnt only when a match is present; the compiler behavior under test is whether GCC preserves that efficient mask-only fast path or needlessly inserts kmov instructions that slow the loop.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer is a vectorized char16_t search loop that processes 32 elements per iteration using two 256-bit loads and two AVX-512 mask-producing equality compares. Its critical fast path is the early branch that decides whether the current 32-element block contains any candidate match; that branch can be done entirely with mask registers via kortestw. GCC generates correct code but eagerly copies both masks from k-registers into general-purpose registers with kmovw before issuing kortestw, even though those scalar copies are only needed later for tzcnt and mask1==0 on the rare match-found path. Because kmovw and kortestw compete for the same execution resources on the target CPU, those extra moves delay the branch and increase loop throughput cost from roughly 2 cycles to 3 cycles per iteration. So the reproducer demonstrates a backend performance bug: unnecessary early mask materialization destroys the efficient mask-only hot path.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a hot inner loop using AVX-512 mask-producing compares followed by an early-exit/continue branch that can be resolved entirely in mask registers. GCC emits correct compare results into k-registers, but then eagerly materializes both masks into GPRs with kmovw before the branch, even though the immediate consumer of the values is kortestw, which directly accepts k-register operands. The scalarized mask values are only needed later on the colder match-handling path for tzcnt and the mask1==0 test. This indicates a backend code-generation/scheduling defect around AVX-512 mask values: GCC is hoisting mask-to-GPR transfers too early, lengthening the dependency chain on the hot no-match path. The failure is therefore not a functional wrong-code issue, but a missed optimization / poor instruction scheduling issue in x86 backend handling of mask registers, likely involving RTL expansion, register allocation, or scheduling/cost modeling for KMOV versus KORTEST in loops.
possible_causes: x86 backend emits premature mask-to-GPR copies for __mmask values, lowering them before all mask-register-only consumers (such as kortestw) are satisfied.
Missed optimization in RTL/combiner/if-conversion that fails to keep the branch test entirely in k-registers and instead scalarizes masks too early because of later tzcnt and integer-zero-test uses.

Register allocation or live-range splitting for AVX-512 mask pseudos is suboptimal, causing GCC to materialize both k-register results into GPRs at their definition point rather than delaying copies to the cold path where scalar use begins.
Instruction scheduling bug in the i386 backend that places KMOVW before KORTESTW despite no true dependency requiring it, increasing critical-path latency in the loop.

Incorrect or incomplete machine description / cost model for AVX-512 mask operations, so GCC does not recognize that KMOVW is expensive on the target and should be sunk past the branch or partially avoided.
Failure to duplicate or sink scalarization into the taken match-found block, i.e. lack of hot/cold path aware code motion for mask values that are only needed after the branch.

Possible deficiency in x86 pattern selection for intrinsics combining compare-mask + kortest + later tzcnt, where the backend does not form an optimal sequence that uses k-registers for control flow and GPRs only for the selected mask actually consumed by tzcnt.
evidence: The emitted sequence shows vpcmpuw producing %k0 and %k1, followed by kmovw %k0,%edx and kmovw %k1,%eax before kortestw %k1,%k0.
The report explicitly states those two KMOVW instructions are not required for the following check, proving the branch could be decided without scalarizing masks first.
Clang generates compare-to-k-registers followed immediately by kortestw and branch, demonstrating a feasible better code sequence for the same semantics.

Later code needs scalar mask values for _tzcnt_u32(mask1), __tzcnt_u16(mask2), and if (mask1 == 0), which explains why GCC may create GPR copies but does not justify placing both copies on the hot path before the branch.
The hot path is the no-match continue case, so any extra instructions before kortestw directly hurt steady-state loop throughput.

LLVM-MCA analysis in the bug report shows GCC's sequence costs about 3 cycles/iteration versus about 2 cycles/iteration for Clang, matching the hypothesis that the unnecessary KMOVW instructions are on the critical path.

The report notes kmovw and kortestw contend for the same execution resource (port 0) on the target CPU, which explains why scheduling the two kmovw instructions before kortestw creates a measurable delay.

ICC emits only one KMOVW and still achieves about 2 cycles/iteration due to overlap, reinforcing that GCC's specific problem is over-eager placement of both mask copies rather than an unavoidable need to scalarize masks.

selected_files.reason: Most suspicious because the bad sequence is centered on AVX-512 mask-producing compare + kortest lowering on x86. The reproducer uses _mm256_cmpeq_epu16_mask and _kortestz_mask16_u8, and the machine description for SSE/AVX/AVX-512 patterns is the most likely place where compare-to-k-register, kortest, and mask materialization patterns interact and permit or encourage the premature kmovw copies.

Likely involved because x86 machine-description patterns outside sse.md can define or constrain mask-register moves, tests, and branching behavior. A suboptimal pattern split or alternative here could force or favor early k-register to GPR transfers before the branch.

The report is explicitly about a scheduling/performance bug on i386/x86, with kmovw and kortestw contending for the same execution port. Target-specific scheduling cost/latency modeling in this file could be missing the pressure or dependency implications that should keep kortestw earlier and sink kmovw off the hot path.

If the RTL already contains both kmovw and kortestw before the branch, the generic scheduler may still be responsible for their final ordering. This pass is a strong candidate for why independent kmovw instructions remain scheduled ahead of the critical kortestw in the loop.

Whether the scheduler can move kortestw ahead of kmovw depends on dependency construction. An overly conservative dependency between mask-to-GPR copies and the mask test, or incomplete modeling of mask-register uses, would directly explain why the hot-path branch test is delayed.

Possible source of the issue if intrinsic expansion or target RTL expansion eagerly scalarizes __mmask values into GPR pseudos as soon as they are produced, instead of preserving k-register values through the branch and only materializing scalar values on the cold path.

The bug report suggests possible live-range or allocation issues for AVX-512 mask pseudos. If IRA handles k-register pseudos poorly, it may encourage immediate copies into GPRs rather than keeping values in mask registers until their scalar uses actually occur.

Late constraint satisfaction and reload decisions can introduce extra moves or choose alternatives that materialize mask values in GPRs too early. Since kmovw is exactly a cross-register-class transfer, LRA is a plausible contributor.

A missed RTL combine opportunity could leave separate kmovw instructions on the hot path instead of preserving a direct kortest on k-registers and sinking scalarization later. This is less likely than x86 backend files but still plausible for the missed optimization aspect.

Post-reload cleanup is a candidate because the final bad sequence may survive only if no late optimization removes or sinks redundant early kmovw copies after register allocation. A missed postreload simplification could explain the retained hot-path penalty.

gcc/haifa-sched.cc.signature: static int model_spill_cost (int cl, int from, int to)
gcc/haifa-sched.cc.summary: Return the cost of increasing the pressure in class CL from FROM to TO. Here we use the very simplistic cost model that every register above sched_class_regs_num[CL] has a spill cost of 1. We could use other measures instead, such as one based on MEMORY_MOVE_COST. However: (1) In order for an instruction to be scheduled, the higher cost would need to be justified in a single saving of that many stalls. This is overly pessimistic, because the benefit of spilling is often to avoid a sequence of several short stalls rather than a single long one. (2) The cost is still arbitrary. Because we are not allocating registers during scheduling, we have no way of knowing for sure how many memory accesses will be required by each spill, where the spills will be placed within the block, or even which block(s) will contain the spills. So a higher cost than 1 is often too conservative in practice, forcing blocks to contain unnecessary stalls instead of spill code. The simple cost below seems to be the best compromise. It reduces the interference with the normal list scheduler, which helps make it more suitable for a default-on option.

Look for instances where we have an instruction that is known to increase register pressure, and whose result is not used immediately. If it is possible to move the instruction downwards to just before its first use, split its lifetime into two ranges. We create a new pseudo to compute the value, and emit a move instruction just before the first use. If, after register allocation, the new pseudo remains unallocated, the function move_unallocated_pseudos then deletes the move instruction and places the computation just before the first use. Such a move is safe and profitable if all the input registers remain live and unchanged between the original computation and its first use. In such a situation, the computation is known to increase register pressure, and moving it is known to at least not worsen it. We restrict moves to only those cases where a register remains unallocated, in order to avoid interfering too much with the instruction schedule. As an exception, we may move insns which only modify their input register (typically induction variables), as this increases the freedom for our intended transformation, and does not limit the second instruction scheduler pass.

Do a very simple CSE pass over the hard registers. This function detects no-op moves where we happened to assign two different pseudo-registers to the same hard register, and then copied one to the other. Reload will generate a useless instruction copying a register to itself. This function also detects cases where we load a value from memory into two different registers, and (if memory is more expensive than registers) changes it to simply copy the first register into the second register. Another optimization is performed that scans the operands of each instruction to see whether the value is already available in a hard register. It then replaces the operand with the hard register if possible, much like an optional reload would.

Try to simplify a single SET instruction. SET is the set pattern. INSN is the instruction it came from. This function only handles one case: if we set a register to a value which is not a register, we try to find that value in some other register and change the set into a register copy.

Try to replace operands in INSN with equivalent values that are already in registers. This can be viewed as optional reloading. For each non-register operand in the insn, see if any hard regs are known to be equivalent to that operand. Record the alternatives which can accept these hard registers. Among all alternatives, select the ones which are better or equal to the one currently matching, where "better" is in terms of '?' and '!' constraints. Among the remaining alternatives, select the one which replaces most operands with hard registers.

The bug is about poor post-reload instruction placement/combination in a hot loop rather than wrong semantics, and this driver is where such decisions are orchestrated.

reviewed_methods.signature: rtx ix86_expand_builtin (tree exp, rtx target, rtx subtarget, machine_mode mode, int ignore)
reviewed_methods.summary: Expand an expression EXP that calls a built-in function, with result going to TARGET if that's convenient (and in mode MODE if that's convenient). SUBTARGET may be used as the target for computing one of EXP's operands. IGNORE is nonzero if the value is to be ignored.
reviewed_methods.reason: Strongest candidate. The bug pattern is premature scalarization of AVX-512 mask values from k-registers to GPRs even though the immediate hot-path consumer is a mask-only kortest. Builtin expansion is exactly where intrinsics like _mm256_cmpeq_epu16_mask, _kortestz_mask16_u8, and later scalar mask uses get lowered into RTL, so a flawed expansion can easily force early kmov materialization that later scheduling cannot undo cleanly.

This is the strongest candidate. The bug is a backend quality issue in final hot-path code shape after registers have been assigned: two kmovw instructions remain before kortestw even though only the cold path needs scalar mask values. A post-reload combine/simplification pass is exactly where GCC could recognize that the branch can stay entirely in k-registers and sink or avoid one/both kmov materializations until the match-found path. Because the problem is not semantic correctness but poor final placement/combination in the inner loop, reload_combine is the most likely best fix location among the listed methods.

reviewed_methods.signature: static rtx_insn * try_combine (rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i0, bool *new_direct_jump_p, rtx_insn *last_combined_insn)
reviewed_methods.summary: Try to combine the insns I0, I1 and I2 into I3. Here I0, I1 and I2 appear earlier than I3. I0 and I1 can be zero; then we combine just I2 into I3, or I1 and I2 into I3. If we are combining more than two insns and the resulting insn is not recognized, try splitting it into two insns. If that happens, I2 and I3 are retained and I1/I0 are pseudo-deleted by turning them into a NOTE. Otherwise, I0, I1 and I2 are pseudo-deleted. Return 0 if the combination does not work. Then nothing is changed. If we did the combination, return the insn at which combine should resume scanning. Set NEW_DIRECT_JUMP_P to true if try_combine creates a new direct jump instruction. LAST_COMBINED_INSN is either I3, or some insn after I3 that has been I3 passed to an earlier try_combine within the same basic block.
reviewed_methods.reason: This is a strong suspect because it is the main RTL combiner that can reshape dataflow between compare-produced mask values, the branch test, and later scalar uses like tzcnt. The bug pattern fits a combine-time profitability/formation mistake: merging or preserving uses in a way that causes both masks to be materialized into GPRs before the branch instead of keeping the branch mask-only and sinking scalarization to the taken path. As the main transformation engine, it is one of the most likely best places to fix the issue.

reviewed_methods.signature: void ix86_expand_branch (enum rtx_code code, rtx op0, rtx op1, rtx label)
reviewed_methods.reason: Very plausible because the observed bad sequence centers on branch formation. If branch expansion fails to preserve a direct k-register test/branch sequence, or introduces scalar temporaries too early around the conditional jump, it would explain why kmovw appears before kortestw on the hot path.

reviewed_methods.signature: int ix86_adjust_cost (rtx_insn *insn, int dep_type, rtx_insn *dep_insn, int cost, unsigned int)
reviewed_methods.summary: This function corrects the value of COST (latency) based on the relationship between INSN and DEP_INSN through a dependence of type DEP_TYPE, and strength DW. It should return the new value. On x86 CPUs this is most commonly used to model the fact that valus of registers used to compute address of memory operand needs to be ready earlier than values of registers used in the actual operation.
reviewed_methods.reason: Good candidate for a scheduling-quality bug. The report is explicitly about KMOVW being scheduled ahead of KORTESTW despite hurting throughput on the target core. If dependency costs or special-case latency modeling for mask ops are missing here, the scheduler may not see the benefit of delaying kmov to the colder path.

reviewed_methods.signature: static bool combine_validate_cost (rtx_insn *i0, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i3, rtx newpat, rtx newi2pat, rtx newotherpat)
reviewed_methods.summary: Subroutine of try_combine. Determine whether the replacement patterns NEWPAT, NEWI2PAT and NEWOTHERPAT are more expensive according to insn_cost than the original sequence I0, I1, I2, I3 and undobuf.other_insn. Note that I0, I1 and/or NEWI2PAT may be NULL_RTX. Similarly, NEWOTHERPAT and undobuf.other_insn may also both be NULL_RTX. Return false if the cost of all the instructions can be estimated and the replacements are more expensive than the original sequence.
reviewed_methods.reason: The reproducer is a performance bug caused by GCC accepting or preserving a more expensive sequence with two early kmovw instructions before kortestw. If combine's cost model undervalues the harm of early mask scalarization, this method could fail to reject an unprofitable transformation. Still, this function only validates aggregate cost after candidate combinations are formed; it is not itself the transformation logic, so it is plausible but not the top fix point.

But this is a generic heuristic layer, and the bug feels more target-specific and mask-operation-specific than a pure ranking problem.
